deep.reconstruction: This page contains no mathematics. It is a fair-copy prose notebook in German Kurrent script: notes on ancient Greek history, probably from a lecture or course, continuing from the previous page (Delian League, Themistocles' ostracism). Its content in order: (1) In Athens after the Persian Wars all branches of culture flourished almost equally. Literature, especially dramatic poetry, was developed. (2) Despite many wars, the Athenians never became a mere soldier-people. Their sense for arts and sciences never died, and they did not lack great generals. (3) Cimon became one of the outstanding men; his teacher Aristides had died (margin date 467). Cimon was a friend of the aristocracy but also won the trust of the other party. He was very liberal and one of the richest citizens. As a general he ranks with the greatest and was never unlucky in war. (4) He sought to continue the war against Persia as the best means of keeping the Greeks united, but had many enemies. (5) In 469 he led a successful expedition to Asia Minor. He sought out the Persian fleet, met it at the river Eurymedon ('in Cilicien'), almost annihilated it, landed, and also defeated the land army. The sentence 'Darauf beschäftigte [er sich mit] der thracischen Halbinsel' continues on the next page. There is no derivation, formula, or computation to reconstruct. The page is unrelated to Lagrange or to mathematics despite the bundle name. The hand is a regular schoolroom Kurrent, and there is no evidence it is Gauss's own work; it may be notes by a family member or student kept among his papers.
errors: Historical (not mathematical): the Eurymedon river is in Pamphylia, not Cilicia.
Historical: the battle of the Eurymedon is usually dated c. 469–466 BC; the notes' 469 is within the conventional range but uncertain.
No mathematical errors are possible, since the page contains no mathematics.
